metaDescription: AprilAire 500M, 600M, 700, 700M and 800 steam plus the DIGI MISTER duct unit compared by gallons per day, control type and install needs for furnace systems.
expertTake: The AprilAire 700 is the pick for large homes with a furnace, because its own fan makes output independent of how hard the blower pushes. The 500M is the sensible entry for an average house, and the 800 steam is for very large homes or heat-pump systems where warm supply air is missing. If you do not have a forced-air duct system, a whole-house humidifier is the wrong tool and a large console is the answer.
introParagraphs: A whole-house humidifier connects to the furnace, the water line and a drain, then puts moisture into the air that the heating system already moves. The result is even humidity in every room with no tank to fill.

The catch is that the machine has to match the house and the furnace. Output, control type and how the unit gets air through the water panel decide whether the humidity really reaches the number you set.

products.name: AprilAire 700 automatic fan-powered whole-house humidifier

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 5,300 sq ft in tight homes

products.description:
The 700 is the fan-powered member of the family. Bypass units borrow the furnace blower's airflow, so their output rises and falls with how hard the system pushes, but the 700 adds its own fan and works independently of that. Output is listed at 18 gallons per day, with coverage up to 5,300 square feet in tightly built homes.

The automatic version carries dual sensors, one indoors for relative humidity and one outdoors for temperature, so the target humidity drops as it gets colder, which limits window condensation. The tradeoff is cost and a more involved installation, since the fan needs power and the unit is larger. Against the 600 it moves more water and does not depend on the furnace blower, and against the 800 steam it has no boiler and no dedicated circuit.

Ownership is a water panel replaced about once per heating season, with hard water shortening its life. Installing and swapping the panel in fall is the easy way to keep it on schedule.
products.bestFor: Large homes with a forced-air furnace where output must not depend on the blower.
pros: Own fan makes output independent of the furnace blower
Outdoor sensor lowers the target as it gets colder
Large coverage in tightly built homes
cons: Needs power and a bigger installation

products.name: AprilAire 700M manual fan-powered humidifier

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 5,300 sq ft in tight homes

products.description:
The 700M is the same fan-powered machine with a manual control instead of the automatic one. A single indoor sensor monitors relative humidity, and you adjust the setting as the weather changes, which is the main chore the automatic version removes.

It is the cheaper route to the same output and the same fan, which suits owners who do not mind turning a dial in November and again in January. The compromise is condensation: without an outdoor sensor, the setting stays where you left it as the temperature drops, and windows can fog. Against the 700 it gives up automatic adjustment in return for a lower price.

Expect to change the water panel every heating season and to turn the humidistat down on the coldest nights.
products.bestFor: Large homes where the owner is happy to adjust the humidistat by hand.
pros: Same 18 gallons per day and own fan as the 700
Lower cost than the automatic model
Fan makes output independent of the blower
cons: Must be adjusted as the weather changes
Windows can fog if the setting is left too high

products.name: AprilAire 500M manual compact bypass humidifier

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 3,600 sq ft in tight homes

products.description:
The 500M is the compact bypass unit and the entry point for an average house. It borrows the furnace blower's airflow to move air through a water panel, so it has no fan of its own and the lowest cost and noise of the family. Output is 12 gallons per day, listed for up to 3,600 square feet in tight homes.

A single indoor sensor gives manual control, so you adjust the setting through the season. The tradeoff is dependence on the blower: when the furnace is idle, no air moves through the panel, and in homes with a weak blower output suffers. Against the 600 it is smaller and lighter on water, and for a typical house that is plenty.

Change the panel once a season, set the damper to summer position in the warm months and keep the HVAC filter clean for airflow.
products.bestFor: Average-size homes with a forced-air furnace and a modest budget.
pros: Lowest cost and size in the AprilAire range
No fan of its own to fail
cons: Output depends on the furnace blower

products.name: AprilAire 600M manual high-output humidifier

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 5,000 sq ft in tight homes

products.description:
The 600M is a bypass unit with a larger water panel, delivering 17 gallons per day for up to 5,000 square feet in tightly built homes. It takes the same installation approach as the 500M but with more capacity.

The larger output is only as good as the blower behind it, because there is still no fan of its own. In a big house with a weak system it will fall short of its rating, which is where the fan-powered 700 earns its premium. It uses the same manual control as the 500M and 700M.

Plan for panel replacement each heating season and use hot water supply to the unit if you can, since that gives the best output.
products.bestFor: Larger homes with a strong furnace blower and a manual preference.
cons: Output still depends on the blower

products.name: AprilAire 800 automatic steam humidifier

specList.label: Coverage
specList.value: Up to 10,300 sq ft in tight homes

products.description:
The 800 is a steam humidifier: it boils water with electrodes and releases steam, so it does not rely on warm air passing through a panel. That makes it the right tool for very large homes and for heat-pump systems, where supply air is not warm enough for an evaporative unit to give full output.

Six output levels let you set capacity to the size of the house, and automatic control uses indoor and outdoor sensors. The costs are the electricity to boil water, a dedicated circuit and mineral scale inside the cylinder, which is a consumable you replace. There is no water panel, but there is a cylinder that needs service in hard water. Against the 700 it handles bigger homes and cooler supply air, at higher running cost.

Have it installed by someone who handles the electrical and plumbing work, and plan for periodic cylinder replacement. Because steam is hot, the distribution tube and mounting location matter, and a poor installation can drip condensate or spit water, so choose a qualified installer rather than relying on a general handyman. In very large homes it can also be a reliable partner for a fan-powered unit on another floor.
products.bestFor: Very large homes and heat-pump systems.
pros: Steam output does not need warm supply air
Six levels sized to the house
cons: Needs a dedicated circuit and boils water
Cylinder wears out in hard water

products.name: DIGI MISTER duct-mount atomizing humidifier
products.description:
The DIGI MISTER takes a different route: instead of a water panel, it sprays a fine mist from nozzles into the warm duct air. You change capacity by using one to five nozzles and by adjusting water pressure, and a patented compact design needs only a small cutout.

There is no wick to replace, and an observation window lets you check the mist visually. Atomizing nozzles can clog with minerals and need cleaning, and the system is less common, so installers and replacement parts are harder to find than for the main brand. Against the AprilAire bypass units it has fewer wearing parts but more fiddly setup.

Use softened or filtered water where you can, and check the nozzles at the start of the season. Because the water is atomized straight into the duct, deposits can build on the duct walls if the setting is too high, so keep the output modest and inspect the duct near the nozzles once a year. This is a system for owners who like tuning things, not for those who want a fit-and-forget panel.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want adjustable capacity and no water panel.
cons: Less common, so parts and installers are scarcer

buyingCriteria.explanation: Bypass units like the 500M and 600M borrow furnace airflow and have no fan, which is cheapest but depends on the blower. A fan-powered unit like the 700 adds its own fan, and a steam unit like the 800 boils water and works with cool supply air. Match the type to your furnace and house size.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Compare gallons per day on the same basis
buyingCriteria.explanation: The 500M lists 12 gallons per day, the 600M 17 and the 700 18. Some brands quote higher figures at a hotter plenum temperature, and the usual rating basis is a stated temperature around 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Compare units on the same basis, and remember that real output depends on the house.

The 500M's 3,600 square feet and the 600M's 5,000 apply to tightly built homes. A leaky older house needs more output than its size suggests, and a very tight house needs less. Treat the coverage as a ceiling and check it against your construction. A house with new windows and sealed ducts holds moisture well, so a smaller unit does the job, while a drafty century-old house loses humidity as quickly as you add it. Count windows, check for gaps around doors and consider the ceiling height, since a tall open-plan house has more air to humidify than the floor area suggests.

A manual unit has one indoor sensor and you adjust it by season, while an automatic unit adds an outdoor sensor so the target drops as it gets colder. That limits window condensation without your help. Manual saves money, automatic saves attention. If you are the kind of person who adjusts the thermostat daily, a manual humidistat will not bother you, but if the unit lives in a basement and you forget it exists, the automatic model protects your windows and your woodwork from the consequences of a setting that no longer suits the weather.

Evaporative units need warm supply air to evaporate water, so heat-pump homes with cooler supply air get less output. Steam units like the 800 solve that, at higher running cost. Ask your installer what your supply air temperature really is. Heat-pump systems often deliver air that is only mildly warm, and an evaporative panel in that stream may produce well under its rated output, so a number on the box is not a promise. A fan-powered unit helps with airflow but not with temperature, which is why steam enters the discussion for those homes.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Budget for the panel and the water
buyingCriteria.explanation: Water panels need replacement about once per heating season, hard water shortens their life and cleaning removes only surface scale. A drain line and a hot water supply give the best output. Count the yearly panel cost as part of ownership, not an afterthought. Installing the unit and swapping the panel are easiest in early fall, before the heating season starts and the furnace is already running, and a spare panel on the shelf means a mid-winter failure never leaves the house dry. If you have a water softener, feed the humidifier from the hot line before the softener where the installer allows it, since softened water can leave a slick residue on some panels.

specDecoder.watchFor: The 500M's 12, 600M's 17 and 700's 18 are rated at a stated plenum temperature.

specDecoder.meaning: The unit has its own fan, so output does not depend on the furnace blower.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 700 and 700M need power for the fan.

specDecoder.watchFor: The 800 has no panel but has a cylinder that wears in hard water.

howWeEvaluated.title: Output and house fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared gallons per day and listed coverage across the lineup. The 700's 18 and the 800's steam levels led, and the 500M's 12 suited average houses. Coverage was treated as a ceiling.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow design
howWeEvaluated.description: Bypass, fan-powered and steam designs were weighed against how well each copes with weak blowers and cool supply air. The 700 and 800 earned credit where the blower is the limit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: Manual and automatic controls were compared. The outdoor sensor on the 700 and 800 earned credit for limiting condensation. Manual models were rated on simplicity and price.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: Panel and cylinder replacement, drain needs and hard water effects were reviewed using owner feedback patterns. The DIGI MISTER lost points for nozzle clogging and scarcer parts.

howWeEvaluated.title: Installation
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted the plumbing, electrical and duct work needed. The bypass units were easiest, the fan-powered units added power, and the steam unit needed a dedicated circuit.

cards.label: Bypass
cards.text: The 500M and 600M have no fan and borrow the furnace blower. They cost less and make less noise, but output depends on the blower.

cards.label: Fan-powered
cards.text: The 700 and 700M add their own fan, so output does not depend on the furnace. They cost more and need power.

howToChoose.note: Choose bypass for a strong system and fan-powered where the blower is weak or the house is large.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A steam design that does not need warm supply air, or a fan-powered unit paired with an installer's confirmation of supply air temperature.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The AprilAire 800 steam works independent of supply air temperature, while evaporative units like the 500M give less output on cool air.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: The house is large, leaky or heated by a heat pump, which points to the 700 or 800.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The house is average and tight, where the 500M is enough.

maintenance.why: Scale clogs the panel and cuts output. Hard water shortens its life.
Mineral deposits block the drain. A vinegar rinse keeps it clear.
The bypass damper should close in warm months. Turn off the water supply too.
A clogged filter reduces airflow and bypass output.
Minerals coat the electrodes. Replace the cylinder when the unit prompts.

faq.q: What is the difference between bypass and fan-powered?
faq.a: A bypass unit uses the furnace blower and has no fan of its own. A fan-powered unit has its own fan, so output does not depend on the furnace.
Typically 30 to 40 percent in winter. Higher causes window condensation and mold risk, especially on cold nights.

faq.q: Do I need a drain line?
faq.a: Yes for most units. Hot water supply and a drain give the best output and keep scale from sitting in the unit.

faq.q: Will it work with a heat pump?
faq.a: Evaporative units give less output on cool supply air. A steam unit like the 800 is designed for that case.

faq.q: How often does the panel need replacing?
faq.a: About once per heating season, sooner in hard water. Cleaning only removes surface scale.

faq.q: Is a whole-house humidifier worth it?
faq.a: In a house with dry winters and a forced-air system, yes, because it humidifies every room without a tank. Without ducts, a large console is the better choice.
